clue.text: Ambassador snatches back dossier, second in existence?

indicators.note: to snatch is to grab and hold, so the ambassador's letters end up clutching the rest

parts.note: His Excellency, the form of address for an ambassador

indicators.note: going back means the dossier and the second are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a dossier is a file of papers
a mo is a moment, a second

explanation.surface: A diplomat grabs a file back from someone, a moment of intrigue in an ambassador's world.
explanation.walkthrough: HE, His Excellency, is the standard form of address for an ambassador; mo is everyday British slang for a moment. 'back' turns both the dossier and the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Domestic life is the everyday way one lives, so the question mark flags a playful, partial sense of being alive.

clue.text: Boss, maybe, whom you ring personally at progressive locations

indicators.note: progressive positions step forward one place each time, so each word yields a letter one further along than the last

parts.note: second letter
third letter
fourth letter
fifth letter

explanation.surface: Advice to phone the boss in person rather than send a message.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' looks like a manager; it is the German fashion label Hugo Boss, so 'maybe' marks HUGO as one possible forename for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The fashion house founded by Hugo Boss carries his full name, so the first name is one example of what precedes that surname.

clue.text: Curious Olivier cameo impresses child performers

indicators.note: to impress is to press something into a surface, so the jumbled letters take another piece inside them
something curious is odd or strange, so the actor's name and his small role come out in an odd order

parts.note: the actor's surname and the word for a brief film appearance, taken letter for letter
ch is the standard abbreviation for child

explanation.surface: A great actor makes a brief, odd appearance alongside a troupe of young stage performers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'child performers' reads as one phrase, but the child is only the inserted CH and 'performers' alone is the definition. Welsh male voice choirs are famous examples.
explanation.definitionFit: A choir of men singing together is a group that gives concerts, so its members are performers.

clue.text: A little latitude given over term of treaty?

definitions.text: A little latitude given over term of treaty?

indicators.note: turned over means flipped end to end, so the preceding letters are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: taken as written
wee is Scots for small
L is the abbreviation for latitude on maps

indicators.note: a term is an end or limit, so only the final letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A negotiator concedes a small amount of flexibility in one clause of an international agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: A WEE L turned round, then the end of treaty, gives LEEWAY, which is exactly a little latitude conceded in a treaty's terms.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeway is room for manoeuvre or freedom of action, which is what negotiators grant when they allow some slack in an agreement.

clue.text: Why buy wrapping paper now?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the reason is to wrap a gift
second meaning: for the time being

explanation.surface: Someone wonders why they should bother buying gift wrap at this moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'now' looks like part of the question about when to shop; it is a separate definition of the phrase as a time expression.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means temporarily or for the time being, and also answers the question with 'to wrap a gift'.

clue.text: Something to inspire sexy guy between foxtrot and tango

indicators.note: only what lies between the two outer NATO letters is kept, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: foxy means sexily attractive
a gent is a man, a guy
Foxtrot is F in the NATO alphabet
Tango is T in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A dance floor scene: an attractive man caught between a foxtrot and a tango.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foxtrot' and 'tango' look like dances, but they are NATO letters marking the ends of the phrase, which are discarded. 'inspire' is used in its literal sense of breathing in.
explanation.definitionFit: To inspire is literally to breathe in, and the gas we take into our lungs for life is the element named.

clue.text: Means to cover boobs — a new cycling trimmer

indicators.note: going round in a cycle moves letters from one end to the other, so the string is rotated to start at a new point

parts.note: Tipp-Ex is the correction fluid painted over mistakes, and boobs are blunders
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: An advert for an underwear product and a new trimmer that runs on a cycle.
explanation.walkthrough: TIPPEXAN is rotated so the X comes to the front. Xantippe (Xanthippe) was the wife of Socrates, proverbial for scolding; a trimmer is an old word for a scold.
explanation.definitionFit: Socrates' wife became a byword for a nagging, shrewish woman, and a trimmer is one who delivers sharp rebukes.

clue.text: Possibly make best start round if e.g. batting?

indicators.note: batting things about knocks them around, so the preceding letters are hit into a new order

parts.note: taken letter for letter
O is round in shape
taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A cricket question: is batting a good way to get the innings off to its best start?
explanation.walkthrough: 'batting' looks like the definition but signals the shuffle. In baseball the batter aims to reach the first of four bases; the phrase means achieve an initial success, and in US slang a first romantic step, hence 'Possibly make'.
explanation.definitionFit: To make it can mean succeed, and the phrase means achieving the first stage of an undertaking, so it may stand for making progress.

clue.text: Sign criminal's rolled off liquor pot

indicators.note: something rolled over is turned head to tail, so the word for a lawbreaker is read from its end

parts.note: a felon is one who commits a serious crime
TT stands for teetotal, abstaining from alcohol
an urn is a vessel or pot

explanation.surface: A drunk lawbreaker has toppled off a pot of booze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off liquor' reads as part of the scene of the fall; it is TT, the abbreviation for teetotal.
explanation.definitionFit: A road sign prohibiting drivers from turning to the left is one of the standard traffic instructions.

clue.text: Flower deity adopting mediaeval king?

indicators.note: to adopt is to take in, so the deity's letters take the other pieces inside

parts.note: a deity is a god
olden means of former times, such as the Middle Ages
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A god taking in a medieval monarch, like a legend of divine adoption.
explanation.walkthrough: 'king' as R comes from the Latin rex, a crossword convention; olden stands for mediaeval as both mean belonging to bygone times.
explanation.definitionFit: Goldenrod is a tall plant with plumes of yellow blooms, a familiar garden and wayside species.

clue.text: On set of Twins cameraman might look back in surprise

definitions.text: On set of Twins cameraman might
definitions.meaning: first meaning: filming a scene twice, once for each of the twin characters
second meaning: react with a delayed second glance of astonishment

explanation.surface: A behind-the-scenes moment on the set of the film Twins, where the camera operator glances back, startled.
explanation.walkthrough: Twins is a 1988 comedy starring Arnold Schwarzenegger and Danny DeVito; a take is one filmed shot, so a film about a pair needs a doubled one.
explanation.definitionFit: A double take is a delayed second look at something unexpected, the classic comic reaction of astonishment.

clue.text: Recognising no limits in a talk about buttocks

indicators.note: accepting no limits means the phrase loses its outer edges and only the letters inside are kept

parts.note: the phrase run together, stripped of its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A speaker who knows no bounds, giving a talk about bottoms.
explanation.walkthrough: Natal here is not the birth word but the anatomical adjective from nates, the buttocks; 'in a talk' without its ends gives it.
explanation.definitionFit: Nates is the anatomical Latin for the rump, and its adjective describes anything concerning the rear end.

clue.text: Source of moving air? A foul, stormy March ahead

indicators.note: a stormy month is turbulent, so its letters are tossed into a new order

parts.note: the month, taken as written before rearranging
an in-off, potting the cue ball off another ball, is a foul in pool and snooker

explanation.surface: A weather note: foul air, as a stormy March blows in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving air' is not wind but a stirring tune; 'ahead' puts the rearranged month in front.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian composer wrote emotionally stirring melodies, and an air is a tune, so he is a creator of touching airs.

clue.text: US-owned property addressing the matter of draught beer, say

parts.note: re means concerning or regarding
ale is beer, often served on draught
to state is to say

explanation.surface: An American-owned pub where the talk turns to the quality of the beer on tap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US-owned' looks like describing a foreign buyer; it tells you the phrase is the usual American term for land and buildings.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans call land and buildings held by someone real estate, where Britons would say property.

clue.text: See 2
Love idol eagerly taken from behind

indicators.note: taking a word from behind means starting at its end and reading backwards

parts.note: sore is an archaic adverb for greatly or keenly, as in 'sore afraid'

explanation.surface: A romantic idol pursued with enthusiasm by an admirer.
explanation.walkthrough: Sore as an old-fashioned intensifier ('I sore desire') is the key; turned round it gives EROS.
explanation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek god of desire, and his statue in Piccadilly Circus makes him an idol in both senses.

clue.text: Somewhat distracted, put Option A

indicators.note: a distracted mind is all over the place, so the following letters are scattered and rearranged

parts.note: the three words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A quiz contestant, only half paying attention, goes for the first choice.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are qualifying phrases meaning partly or to a limited degree, interchangeable in a sentence about agreeing.

clue.text: Lasting until dawn in ships lightermen unloaded

indicators.note: to ship is to carry as cargo, so the first piece carries the second on board

parts.note: a fire that is in is burning, alight

indicators.note: an unloaded vessel has had its contents removed, so only the shell of the word is kept

parts.note: just the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Bargemen work right through the night emptying the ships.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a link word; it is the definition-style sense of a fire that is in, alight. Lightermen work barges called lighters that unload ships.
explanation.definitionFit: Something all-night goes on through the whole of the hours of darkness, continuing until morning.

clue.text: Neighbourhood meeting sculptor held for bishop in centre of hall

indicators.note: something held for another stands in its place, so the artist's name replaces the churchman

parts.note: a lobby is an entrance hall
Alexander Calder, the American sculptor of mobiles
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A community gathering where an artist replaces the bishop in the middle of the village hall.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the central bishop of the hall word is replaced; Alexander Calder was the American who invented the mobile. A local derby is a match between two teams from the same town.
explanation.definitionFit: A game between near rivals is a clash of neighbours, so a fixture of this kind is a meeting of the neighbourhood.

clue.text: Hats off to synod, appointing radical figure of authority

indicators.note: hats sit on top, so taking the hats means taking the topmost letter of each word

parts.note: first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter

explanation.surface: Churchmen doff their hats to a church council that has chosen a radical leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hats off' reads like a salute; here it means take the heads of the next four words.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsar was the Russian emperor, and the word is now used for any official given sweeping powers.

clue.text: Prepare to drive towards green Chesterfield?

parts.note: to set is to make ready
in golf a tee is where you drive from towards the green

explanation.surface: A golfer gets ready to hit off at a course in Chesterfield.
explanation.walkthrough: Chesterfield looks like the Derbyshire town; it is a deep-buttoned leather sofa, and the question mark shows it is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A chesterfield is a padded sofa with arms and back of the same height, one kind of couch.

clue.text: Several drinks do take out reserves

indicators.note: to drink is to take in, so the number swallows the following words

parts.note: seven is a number that counts as several
to do someone is to cheat or con them
dele is the proofreader's mark for delete

explanation.surface: A party where several drinks are had and then a takeaway is ordered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drinks' is a verb here, not the noun it seems. Dele is the proofreader's instruction to delete. A second eleven is a club's reserve cricket or football team.
explanation.definitionFit: A club's back-up side is made up of the players held in reserve behind the first team.

clue.text: See 7
Parody of Hell's Kitchen

indicators.note: of here means taken from, so the letters come out of the following words

parts.note: running across the apostrophe-s and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: A comic send-up of the reality show Hell's Kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: A short comic sketch that mocks something is a light satirical piece, a send-up.

clue.text: One or more of Damon Gough's tapes

indicators.note: to tape is to record, so the name's letters hold the answer recorded within them

parts.note: inside the singer's name, running across the space

explanation.surface: A fan pulls out a few of the recordings by Damon Gough, the musician known as Badly Drawn Boy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something counted among a group is one of its members, so the preposition stands for being part of a set.

clue.text: What breakfast waiter brings forward when beat?

parts.note: to as in 'to and fro', moving forward
as means when, as in 'as I left'
a beat or track is a regular path or route

explanation.surface: A hotel waiter rushing out with the breakfast order when he's tired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beat' looks like 'exhausted'; it is a route, as in a policeman's beat.
explanation.definitionFit: Hotel breakfast service brings toast to the table standing upright in a little holder.

clue.text: In the course of a number of years, singer slips

indicators.note: something happening in the course of a period falls within it, so one word lies inside the other

parts.note: an era is a span of years
a singer is an informer, one who sings to the police, as is a rat

explanation.surface: Over the years a vocalist has made mistakes on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'singer' looks musical; in crime slang it is a grass or informer.
explanation.definitionFit: Errata are listed mistakes in a printed book, and slips is a common word for small errors.

clue.text: Passionate old soldier subdues macho types

indicators.note: to subdue is to hold down and keep under control, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: a vet is a veteran
he-men are muscular macho men

explanation.surface: A fiery veteran keeps a group of tough guys in line.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe strong feeling forcefully expressed, as in an intense, fervent protest or argument.
